chapters.title: External Calendars
chapters.subtitle: Show another calendar's events in yours, read only

steps.text: External Calendars show the events of another calendar inside one of yours, kept up to date by the site. This video shows how to subscribe a calendar to an iCalendar address, how often it is read, what the events look like, and what happens when an address cannot be used.

chapters.title: Why external calendars
chapters.subtitle: See other people's calendars next to your own

steps.text: Partners, vendors and other teams publish their calendars somewhere else. You want to see them next to your own events, without copying anything by hand.
With the External Calendars feature on, a calendar can follow a secret iCalendar address, such as the one Google Calendar or Outlook shows in a calendar's settings.
The events are copied in, kept up to date, and removed here when they are removed there. They cannot be changed here, because the other calendar owns them.
Signing in to Google Calendar or Microsoft 365 to keep calendars in step both ways is not available. The address is the only link.

chapters.title: Subscribe a calendar
chapters.subtitle: An address, and how often to read it

steps.text: Open Manage Calendars, and add a General calendar. Name it Partner events. Its editor has a Subscription card, with a box to keep this calendar in step with an external calendar. Tick it.
Keep the provider on iCalendar address, and paste the external calendar's address. It must start with https, http or webcal.
Every sets how often the calendar is read, at least every five minutes. The site looks for calendars that are due once every five minutes. Choose Save.
Now try an address that cannot be used, one on this same machine. Add another calendar, Broken feed, with a page of this site as its address, and save it.

chapters.title: What happens next
chapters.subtitle: Events arrive, and failures are explained

steps.text: A few minutes later, the first read has happened. Open the Partner events calendar, and look at the Subscription card. Last synchronized shows when it last worked, and what it did.
Open the calendar. The partner's events are here, in the calendar's color.
Click an event. You can read it, but there is no Edit button, because the other calendar owns it. Change it there, and it changes here at the next read.
Now the broken feed. Its Last synchronized shows why it failed. Addresses on the local network cannot be subscribed to, so a calendar cannot be used to reach private systems on your network.

After each failure in a row, the site waits longer before it tries again, up to thirty-two times the interval. The events already in the calendar stay, and one failing address never blocks the others.
Use the address the other calendar publishes for sharing, and treat it like a password. Anyone who has it can read that calendar.
The address must be reachable from the internet. Addresses on private or local networks are refused.
To stop following a calendar, untick the box. Subscribing is one direction only, and nothing you do here changes the other calendar.
Paste a calendar's address, and its events appear in yours and stay up to date. Thanks for watching.
